d3.overview: Domain III is the development half of the AI lifecycle: how an organization governs the designing and building of an AI system, the collection and use of data to train and test it, and its release, monitoring and maintenance. It carries 21 to 25 of the 100 scored items, among the heaviest of the four domains, and it is where governance stops being policy and becomes engineering practice.
d3.deep_dive:
Domain III covers the build. Domain I asked what AI governance is; Domain II asked what the law requires; Domain III asks how the organization runs the process - what it decides, what it writes down, and who signs off. It carries 21 to 25 of the 100 scored items and splits into three competencies of near-equal weight.

| Competency | Subject | Questions |
|---|---|---|
| **III.A** | Govern designing and building the AI system | 6 to 8 |
| **III.B** | Govern data collection and use in training and testing | 6 to 8 |
| **III.C** | Govern release, monitoring and maintenance | 8 to 10 |

### The organizing idea: a chain of documented decisions

Almost every Domain III item is a question about process discipline. A use case drives an impact assessment; the assessment drives requirements and design; the design drives what data is needed; data governance decides whether that data may be used; testing decides whether the build is fit; a readiness gate decides whether it ships; monitoring decides whether it keeps working. Each link produces a record, and the record is what the organization is asked for in an audit or a regulatory request. That is why documenting the design and build process, and the training and testing process, are BOK performance indicators in their own right: traceability is the deliverable, not a by-product.

### What each competency tests

**III.A** is intent and foresight: a use case with boundaries, success metrics and decision rights; an impact assessment that captures benefits as well as harms and records residual risk with the approver who accepted it; and the split between internal design risk (faulty assumptions, inadequate data, incomplete testing, poor integration, no explainability) and external risk (adversarial use, regulatory change, supply chain, backlash). The named techniques are the probability/severity matrix, the risk mitigation hierarchy, stakeholder mapping, use case evaluation, benchmarking, and pre-deployment pilots.

**III.B** is data and evidence: a defendable legal right to use the data first, then quality on accuracy, completeness, integrity, timeliness, consistency, sufficiency and representativeness. Provenance (origin and terms) is separated from lineage (every transformation to the model version). Then the testing regime: unit, integration, validation, performance, security, bias and interpretability, each tied to the risk it catches.

**III.C** is release and drift: readiness as model card, conformity evidence, stress and failover testing, and a multidisciplinary gate review; deployment that is traceable, repeatable and reversible, with environment separation, rollback procedures and a model registry; monitoring of prediction quality, inputs, latency, resources, fairness and drift on a retraining schedule set by volatility and risk.

### The standards and legal layer

ISO/IEC 42001 is the certifiable AI management system and requires an AI system impact assessment (clauses 6.1.4 and 8.4; Annex A objective A.5). ISO/IEC 42005 explains how to run one, and it is guidance only: nothing is certified to 42005. ISO/IEC 23894 manages risk to the organization's own objectives, while 42005 looks outward at the people affected. The NIST AI RMF supplies MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE and GOVERN plus the TEVV discipline of keeping verifiers separate from builders; NIST SP 1270 supplies the three bias categories.

For high-risk systems the EU AI Act makes much of this law: Article 9 (risk management), Article 10 (data governance), Article 11 and Annex IV (technical documentation), Article 14 (human oversight), Article 15 (accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity), Article 17 (quality management system), Article 43 (conformity assessment) and Article 72 (post-market monitoring). An organization that builds and releases its own high-risk model is the provider, and those duties cannot be handed to a supplier.

Expect process questions: which artifact does this stage produce, which review gate applies, who signs off, what triggers a reassessment. The BOK names the techniques directly (probability/severity matrix, risk mitigation hierarchy, stakeholder mapping, benchmarking, pre-deployment pilots), so learn them by name. BOK v2.1 removed the "identify applicable laws" indicator from III.A, which means legal applicability is tested in Domain II, not here; a Domain III stem that quotes a statute is usually testing the process obligation that statute imposes, not the statute itself.

ch10.overview: III.C governs the back of the lifecycle: deciding the system is ready to release, moving it into production under policy and change control, and keeping it accurate, fair and secure afterwards through continuous monitoring, periodic assessment and a scheduled maintenance and retraining cadence, with incidents managed and documented.
ch10.deep_dive:
III.C carries 8 to 10 questions, the heaviest competency in the exam, and it is where governance becomes operations.

### 1. Pre-release readiness

A production readiness evaluation covers safety, accountability, suitability for the intended context, regulatory conformity, benchmarking and operational planning. The **model card** is the headline artifact: intended and out-of-scope uses, how the model was evaluated, performance across relevant groups and conditions, and known limitations. Operational readiness means stress testing under expected and edge-case workloads: latency and throughput benchmarks, memory and compute use under load, failover behaviour during outages, and evaluation against adversarial and malicious prompts. Release runs through change management with release, verification and rollback procedures, then staged rollouts behind feature flags, canary deployments, KPI and leading risk indicator monitoring, and clear escalation channels. The final gate is a multidisciplinary review: legal on data use and licensing, engineering on technical validation and scalability, business on value alignment, cybersecurity on vulnerabilities, privacy on data use, governance on fairness, accountability and transparency.

### 2. Deployment

Deployment is a governance transition, not just a technical milestone: responsibility moves from the development team to operations. Policy needs approval gates, strict release procedures (developers do not hold production admin), mandatory isolation between development, staging and production, and rollback procedures. Deployment must be **traceable, repeatable and reversible**, which is what version control, CI/CD logging and a model registry are for. Data governance continues into production: minimization, purpose limitation, retention limits, fine-grained access controls on real-time inputs, and input quality monitoring.

User training is part of the control set, including role-based instruction, administrative training, and confidence thresholding so people know when not to trust the output. ### 3. Continuous monitoring

Monitoring areas: prediction quality (accuracy, precision, recall, confidence), data inputs (volume, format, anomalies, missing values, prompt injection, poisoning), latency and throughput, resource consumption, fairness across subgroups, drift, and usage metrics such as adoption and abandonment. The infrastructure is transaction logging, dashboards, threshold alerts and audit logs, and the higher goal is **observability**: being able to say why the model produced a given output, not just that it did.

Drift comes in three shapes and the exam tests the labels. **Covariate drift** is a change in the input distribution, **label drift** a change in the distribution of outcomes, and **concept drift** a change in the relationship between inputs and outputs (fraud tactics evolving is the standard example). Detection uses statistical tests such as Kolmogorov-Smirnov or the population stability index, prediction monitoring for confidence drops, and shadow models trained on recent data for comparison.

Fairness can degrade after release even when the model passed pre-release checks, so subgroup performance, complaints, appeal outcomes and override logs are ongoing signals. Maintenance schedules set cadence by volatility and risk: regular evaluation, scheduled retraining from weekly to annually, immediate hotfixes, quarterly business reviews, and dependency and compliance updates. Tripwires that force a review or suspension include a rapid rise in edge-case failures, repeated human overrides, declining engagement, more toxic or hallucinated output, and more abuse cases.
ch10.exam: Eight to ten questions, the largest single block in the exam. The reliable anchors are the artifact-to-stage mapping (model card at readiness, model registry at deployment, audit log and dashboard in monitoring) and the three drift labels. Expect a stem where a model passes pre-release fairness testing and then degrades in production, testing whether you know fairness is monitored rather than assumed. Also expect the traceable, repeatable, reversible triad, and the distinction between a fail-safe plan, which is a pre-decided fallback, and a rollback procedure, which reverses a release. For high-risk systems the EU AI Act makes several of these duties explicit: Article 15 for robustness and fail-safe redundancy, Article 43 for conformity assessment, Article 72 for post-market monitoring and Article 73 for serious incident reporting.

t_monitoring.overview: Deployment starts a new operational phase rather than ending governance. Continuous monitoring watches prediction quality, inputs, latency, resources, fairness, drift and usage; operational controls decide what happens when a threshold is crossed; and a maintenance schedule sets the cadence for evaluation, retraining and dependency updates. The three drift types are the vocabulary the exam tests.
t_monitoring.deep_dive:
### What continuous monitoring covers

Prediction quality (accuracy, precision, recall, confidence); data inputs (volume, format, anomalies, missing values, prompt injection, model poisoning); latency and performance under varying load; resource consumption (CPU, GPU, memory, storage, network); fairness across subgroups over time; drift in data distribution or model output; and usage metrics such as adoption rates, abandonment and user behaviour. The higher goal is **observability**: being able to say why a model produced a given output, which requires traceable prediction paths, logged model versions and configuration, and correlation of outputs with inputs.

### Drift, by name

**Data drift** is a change in the statistical properties of input data over time, so production data diverges from training data. The finer taxonomy distinguishes **covariate drift** (the input distribution changes, for example new customer behaviours), **label drift** (the distribution of outcomes changes, for example loan defaults rise) and **concept drift** (the relationship between inputs and outputs changes, which is what happens when fraud tactics evolve so the old patterns no longer predict the new fraud). Detection uses statistical tests such as Kolmogorov-Smirnov or the population stability index, prediction monitoring for sharp drops in confidence or consistency, and shadow models trained on recent data for comparison against production.

### Fairness, ethics and emerging risk

Fairness can degrade after release even when the model passed pre-release fairness testing, so monitoring tracks prediction patterns across sensitive attributes, watches for subgroup degradation, reviews user complaints and appeal outcomes, and monitors transparency. Ethical indicators include surges in opt-outs or complaints, increases in flagged content, and escalation logs showing overrides or rollbacks. The discipline the note insists on is monitoring **all aspects of any business process enabled by AI**, not only the model: the surrounding workflow can fail while the model behaves. Leading indicators that should trigger review or suspension include a rapid rise in edge-case failures, repeated human overrides of predictions, declining user trust or engagement, rising toxicity, misinformation or hallucination, and a rapid increase in abuse cases. Governance teams maintain **tripwires** that force a review, and any occurrence in these areas is treated as an incident.

### Operational controls

**Operational controls** are the policies, procedures and technical mechanisms governing how the system behaves in production: access controls, monitoring thresholds and intervention protocols, plus AI-specific additions such as alerting for unusual model behaviour, failsafe defaults that deny by default, shadow-mode deployment to test before production, and a kill switch to disable a faulty model. ### Maintenance, retraining and feedback

A **maintenance schedule** sets cadence by volatility and risk: quarterly or monthly model quality evaluation, scheduled retraining from weekly to annually depending on how fast the environment moves, immediate hotfix intervals for urgent failures, quarterly business reviews of metrics, KPIs and incidents, and dependency and compliance updates including regulatory reassessment. **Retraining** updates a trained model with other training data, and it trades accuracy gains against infrastructure cost and freshness against the risk of instability. **Feedback loops** are the structural risk underneath all of this: when a system's outputs influence the future inputs it learns from, bias and error can amplify over time, which is why circuit-breakers and feedback monitoring are part of the control set rather than an afterthought. Where a third party operates the system, visibility drops, so specific contractual terms and periodic audits of the vendor's environment are the mitigation.

Expect the point that fairness must be monitored after release because it can degrade even when pre-release testing passed, and the point that monitoring covers the whole business process, not just the model. Retraining cadence is driven by volatility and risk, and feedback loops are the amplification mechanism that circuit-breakers exist to stop. For high-risk systems, Article 72 is the provider's post-market monitoring duty.

term:Retraining.deep_dive:
ISO/IEC 22989 defines retraining as updating a trained model through training with other training data, and notes the triggers: data drift, concept drift, or insufficient initial data. The standard also flags the risk, catastrophic forgetting, which is why a retrained model is not automatically an improvement and has to be validated like a new one.

The governance frame is that retraining is a governed event, not a background process. The vault note sets out what that means in practice: triggers defined in advance, new versions validated as new models would be, regression-tested against prior behaviour so that the fix for one failure does not introduce another, and documented for the audit trail. A model registry entry recording the new version, the data used and the evaluation results is what makes the change auditable.

Two legal points decide the harder exam items. First, the EU AI Act treats retraining as a life cycle event that feeds the provider's post-market monitoring under Article 72 and the risk-management system under Article 9, so a materially changed high-risk system may need its conformity position re-examined before it ships; Article 111(2) catches systems already on the market only where their design changes significantly. Second, retraining on production data is a new processing purpose. If that data is personal data, GDPR Article 6 requires a lawful basis for the reuse, and purpose limitation under Article 5(1)(b) means the original collection purpose may not cover it. The vault note's tradeoffs table adds the operational tension: accuracy against infrastructure cost, freshness against instability, legal obligations against business priorities.

The exam distinction: retraining is the update itself, while continuous learning is the ISO 22989 special case where it happens incrementally and repeatedly during operation, which raises verification problems because there is no discrete release to validate.
term:Retraining.exam_tip: Retraining is a governed event: defined triggers, validation like a new model, regression testing, documentation. Continuous learning is the ISO 22989 special case of high-frequency retraining during operation. Retraining on production personal data needs a GDPR Article 6 basis.

term:Operational Controls.deep_dive:
Operational controls are the running-state safeguards, and ISO/IEC 42001 is where they are formalised: the AI management system's Annex A control set covers access control on models, data and endpoints, change management for updates, logging and audit trails, monitoring thresholds and alerting, incident procedures, and backup and recovery. The vault note's deployment policy adds the environment controls that make them work: mandatory isolation between development, staging and production, approval gates contingent on prior signoffs, release procedures under which developers do not hold admin access to production, and rollback procedures with escalation contacts.

The distinction from design controls is the useful frame. Design controls prevent a bad system being built; operational controls keep a good system governed once it is running. Both are needed, and the exam tests whether a scenario's problem is a control that was never designed or a control that stopped working.

Two AI-specific wrinkles. Access control has to reach further than the database: prompts, model endpoints, feature stores, training environments and the model registry are all assets. And logging is a statutory control, not only an operational one: Article 12 requires high-risk systems to record events automatically over their lifetime, Article 19 requires the provider to keep those logs for at least six months, and the deployer keeps logs under Article 26(6). That makes log configuration and retention a compliance setting rather than an engineering preference.

The exam distinction: operational controls are the policies, procedures and technical mechanisms governing how the system functions in production, and the four that recur in scenarios are access control, change management, logging and incident response.
term:Operational Controls.exam_tip: Operational controls are the running-state safeguards in ISO/IEC 42001 Annex A: access control, change management, logging, monitoring thresholds, incident response and backup. Their AI-specific reach covers prompts, endpoints, feature stores and the model registry.

term:Maintenance Schedule.deep_dive:
The vault note gives the cadence exam items draw on: regular evaluation quarterly or monthly, scheduled retraining from weekly to annually depending on volatility and risk, immediate hotfix intervals for urgent failures, quarterly business reviews of metrics and incidents, and dependency and compliance updates covering libraries, frameworks, container images and periodic regulatory reassessment. The schedule is a risk decision rather than a default: a high-volume system in a fast-moving environment may need monthly retraining with human validation, while a stable low-stakes classifier may need an annual review.

The governing logic is that a schedule set by the calendar alone is not a control. The vault note's retraining tradeoffs table makes the tension explicit: accuracy improvements against infrastructure costs, need for freshness against risk of instability, legal obligations against business priorities. That is why the schedule is paired with triggers. The vault note's leading indicators are the trigger list: a rapid increase in edge case failures, repeated human overrides of predictions, declining user trust or engagement, rising toxicity, misinformation or hallucination, and a rapid increase in misuse cases. Governance teams maintain tripwires that force a review or suspension, and any occurrence is treated as an incident.

The legal hooks run through the EU AI Act's life cycle duties. Article 72 post-market monitoring is where the schedule's findings feed, and Article 9 requires the risk-management system to keep operating, which means reassessing after changes. Under ISO/IEC 42001 the schedule is documented information the AI management system maintains, and any change to a deployed high-risk system has to be assessed before it ships.

The exam distinction: the maintenance schedule is the planned cadence, the tripwires are the event-driven triggers, and both feed the same review and retraining pipeline.

term:Feedback Loop.deep_dive:
A feedback loop exists when a system's outputs become inputs to its own future operation, either directly or through the world. The vault note frames it as the risk that outputs amplify biases or errors over time and calls for monitoring and circuit-breaking mechanisms. The mechanism matters more than the label: a loop converts a small, tolerable error into a large one without any code change and without a single triggering event, which is why conventional change control never sees it.

Concrete examples make it legible. A predictive policing model that sends patrols to the neighbourhoods it flagged generates more arrests there, which then becomes training data confirming the original flag. A recommendation system that promotes content it predicts will engage trains the next model on behaviour its own promotion produced. A resume screener trained on the outcomes of its own earlier shortlists learns its own preferences back. In each case the loop closes by treating production outcomes as ground truth, which is the same assumption that makes historical labels a fairness risk in supervised learning.

The legal hook is explicit. EU AI Act Article 15 requires high-risk systems to be designed and developed so that they can mitigate feedback loops that would entrench bias or degrade performance across the life cycle, which puts loop mitigation alongside accuracy and robustness as a design requirement rather than an operational nicety. NIST AI 600-1 names homogenization and feedback as a generative-AI risk, and GDPR Article 22 is engaged where the loop drives automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.

The exam distinction: a feedback loop is a structural property of how the system is wired into its environment, whereas drift is a change in the data. Breaking the loop is a design decision, such as holding the model's own outputs out of training or injecting fresh ground truth, not a monitoring setting.
term:Feedback Loop.exam_tip: A feedback loop closes when outputs become training inputs, so errors amplify without any code change. Article 15 requires mitigating them as a design property, and the fix is breaking the loop by holding out self-generated data, not simply monitoring harder.

term:Data Drift.deep_dive:
Data drift is the umbrella term for production data diverging from the data the model was trained on. The vault note splits it into covariate drift (the input distribution changes, for example new customer behaviours or a new device population) and label drift (the distribution of outcomes changes, for example loan defaults rise), with concept drift as the third and most serious case where the input-to-output relationship itself moves.

The mechanism is why drift is a governance problem rather than a maintenance nuisance: nothing in the code changed, so conventional software change control sees no event, yet performance has degraded. The statistical detectors are Kolmogorov-Smirnov and the Population Stability Index, which compare production inputs against the training baseline, alongside prediction monitoring for sharp drops in confidence or consistency and shadow models trained on recent data.

Obligations attach at both ends. Article 26 requires the deployer of a high-risk system to ensure input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose, a duty that decays as the world moves; Article 72 requires the provider's post-market monitoring to catch the resulting degradation. The vault note's data governance activities in the deployment phase are the preventive layer: data quality monitoring that validates inputs and detects anomalies to stop cascading errors, access controls on real-time feeds, and retention and purpose-limitation rules.

Privacy runs in parallel. Production data is frequently personal data, so using it to retrain is a new processing purpose that needs a lawful basis under GDPR Article 6 and may engage Article 22 if it feeds decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.

The exam distinction: data drift is the general phenomenon, covariate and label drift are its measurable forms, and drift detection is a monitoring control rather than a retraining decision.
term:Data Drift.exam_tip: Data drift is the general phenomenon; covariate drift (inputs move) and label drift (outcomes move) are the measurable forms, with concept drift as the relationship change. Article 26 puts the input-data duty on the deployer, and retraining on drifted data needs a GDPR basis.

term:Continuous Monitoring.deep_dive:
Continuous monitoring is the operational phase duty, and the exam splits it by who owes it. Under the EU AI Act the provider owes a post-market monitoring system under Article 72: proportionate to the nature and risks of the system, documented as a plan inside the Article 17 quality management system, collecting and reviewing performance data from use, looking for evidence that the system no longer meets the Chapter III requirements, and feeding findings back into the Article 9 risk-management system. The deployer owes a separate duty under Article 26(5) to monitor operation, tell the provider about risks and cooperate. Article 12 automatic logging is a third, distinct duty, with a retention floor of at least six months under Article 19.

What gets monitored is wider than accuracy, and the vault note's table is the checklist: prediction quality, data inputs (including prompt injection and poisoning attempts), latency, resource consumption, fairness across subgroups, drift, and usage metrics. The infrastructure is transaction logging, dashboards, threshold alerts and audit logs, with observability as the goal, meaning the ability to explain why a given output or failure occurred rather than only that it did. Tooling in common use includes Prometheus, Grafana and the ELK stack, with ML-specific monitors such as Evidently, WhyLabs and SageMaker Model Monitor.

The governance distinction the exam tests is the three-layer split: Article 12 logging records events automatically; Article 26(5) deployer monitoring watches operation and escalates; Article 72 provider post-market monitoring is the structured, documented surveillance programme. As amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI, the Commission must publish guidance and a template for the Article 72 plan by 2 September 2027.

term:Concept Drift.deep_dive:
Concept drift is the drift type that changes the target relationship itself, and the vault note's example is the clearest available: fraud tactics evolve, so the mapping from transaction features to fraudulent or legitimate changes even though the features arrive in much the same distribution. That separates it from covariate drift (the input distribution moves, for example new customer behaviours) and label drift (the distribution of outcomes moves, for example loan defaults rise). Covariate and label drift are about distributions you can measure directly; concept drift is about the relationship, which you can only see through degraded performance.

That difference sets the detection method. Covariate drift is caught by comparing production input distributions against the training baseline, using statistical tests such as Kolmogorov-Smirnov or the Population Stability Index. Concept drift is caught by watching performance against ground truth as it arrives, by monitoring for sharp drops in confidence or consistency, and by shadow models trained on recent data and compared against the production model. A monitoring plan that checks only input distributions will miss concept drift until the labels catch up, which in slow-label settings can take months.

The legal hooks sit in EU AI Act Article 15, which requires high-risk systems to maintain accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity across the life cycle, to be resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies, and to mitigate feedback loops that would otherwise entrench drift. The NIST AI RMF puts the same duty in its Measure and Manage functions, and the vault note treats drift as a leading indicator that should trigger a model review or suspension.

The exam distinction: data drift is the umbrella term for distribution change, concept drift is the specific change in the input-to-output relationship, and retraining is the remedy rather than the detection method.
term:Concept Drift.exam_tip: Concept drift is a change in the input-to-output relationship (fraud tactics evolve), distinct from covariate drift (inputs move) and label drift (outcomes move). It surfaces through performance rather than input statistics alone, and Article 15 requires mitigating feedback loops.

t_deployment.overview: Deployment is the governance transition from development to operations. It covers environment choice (cloud, on-premises, edge, hybrid), optimization decisions (as-is, fine-tuned, RAG, quantized), the policy controls that make a release traceable, repeatable and reversible, conformity requirements, and the liability exposure that follows a system into production, including product liability for defects.
t_deployment.deep_dive:
### Where and how to deploy

**Cloud** scales easily and integrates through APIs but gives less control over data locality and can raise regulatory questions. **On-premises** gives control and suits sensitive data but costs more and scales less. **Edge** gives ultra-low latency and works without a network, at the cost of compute limits and model size constraints. **Hybrid** balances performance and compliance by running inference close to the user and training or updates in the cloud, at the cost of architectural complexity. The decision belongs in the **design phase**, not at release, because it determines what testing and controls are possible.

The optimization decision is separate: deploy the base model **as-is**, **fine-tune** it on domain data (better domain performance, more maintenance and retraining burden), or augment it with **retrieval augmented generation**, which grounds answers in an external knowledge base and reduces hallucination. ### Policy, traceability and reversibility

An effective deployment policy has approval gates contingent on prior compliance, legal and security signoffs; strict release procedures where developers do not hold production admin and the packaged system is handed to operations; mandatory isolation between development, staging and production; and rollback procedures with escalation contacts and fail-safe steps. Deployment must be **traceable, repeatable and reversible**, which is what version control, CI/CD logging and a **model registry** deliver: the registry tracks versions, training data lineage, metadata, deployment status, ownership and contacts, so reproducibility is a lookup rather than a reconstruction.

### Conformity requirements

**Conformity requirements** are the standards, regulations and internal policies a system must satisfy before deployment. Under the EU AI Act the provider of a high-risk system completes a conformity assessment, draws up technical documentation, issues the EU declaration of conformity and applies CE marking before placing it on the market. Obligations then follow the value chain: importers, distributors and authorized representatives carry their own duties (Articles 22 to 24), and Article 25 can push provider obligations onto a distributor, importer or deployer that substantially modifies the system or puts it into service under its own name. Deployers have their own set: using the system per the instructions for use, human oversight, input data relevance, logging, informing workers and affected persons, and cooperating with authorities (Article 26).

### Defects and liability

**Manufacturing defect** is a product liability category: the product deviates from its intended design during production. For AI it maps onto deployment-stage failures such as a corrupted model artifact, a misconfigured pipeline, or a version shipped that was not the version tested. The revised Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853 modernized the EU regime for software and AI, adding disclosure duties and presumptions of defectiveness and causality in cases of technical or scientific complexity, and it sits alongside the other defect categories of design defect and failure to warn or insufficient instructions. ### People and partners

User training is part of the control set for internal users, with role-based and administrative instruction, confidence thresholding so people know when to intervene, job aids, and refreshed enablement as models change. Customer-facing systems owe disclosure of AI capabilities, plain-language description, and notice-and-consent. Where an **AI partner** collaborates in development or deployment, the governance obligations do not transfer: contractual terms, audit rights and periodic assessment of the partner's environment are how accountability stays with the deploying organization.

The triad to memorize is traceable, repeatable and reversible. On conformity, know that Article 25 can move provider duties onto a deployer who substantially modifies a system or puts it into service under its own name, and that Article 26 is the deployer's own obligation set. Manufacturing defect is the product liability category for production-stage deviation from design.

term:Manufacturing Defect.deep_dive:
A manufacturing defect is the product liability theory that the product departed from its intended design during production. It is the middle of three theories: a design defect says the design itself was unreasonably dangerous, a manufacturing defect says the design was fine but this unit was built wrong, and failure to warn says the instructions or warnings were inadequate.

Applied to AI the category is narrower than students expect, and that is the exam point. A model that behaves badly because its training data was unrepresentative or its architecture was a poor choice is a design defect allegation, not a manufacturing defect. A manufacturing defect in an AI context means the artifact that reached production differs from the artifact that was validated: a corrupted or mis-serialised model weight file, a build that shipped the wrong model version, a deployment configuration that silently changed behaviour, or a fine-tune applied in the pipeline that was never assessed. The vault note captures it as deployment errors or corrupted models, which is exactly the version-control and model-registry failure the deployment controls exist to prevent.

The EU frame is the revised Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853, adopted 23 October 2024, in force 8 December 2024, with Member State transposition by 9 December 2026. It treats software including AI as a product irrespective of how it is supplied, and AI Act providers are treated as manufacturers. Liability is no-fault: the claimant proves defect, damage and causation, and Article 10 supplies rebuttable presumptions of defect and causation where technical or scientific complexity makes proof excessively difficult, with machine learning named as an example.

The governance consequence is that configuration control is a liability control. If you cannot show the version in the field is the version you validated, you cannot rebut a manufacturing defect claim.
term:Manufacturing Defect.exam_tip: Manufacturing defect means the unit departed from the validated design: wrong model version, corrupted weights, unassessed pipeline change. Unrepresentative training data or a poor architecture is a design defect instead. The revised PLD treats AI as a product and AI Act providers as manufacturers.

term:Deployment.deep_dive:
ISO/IEC 22989 makes Deployment a named phase of the AI system life cycle, sitting between Verification and Validation and Operation and Monitoring, and defines it as integration into the operational environment plus user training. The inclusion of user training is not incidental: a system is deployed when the people who operate it can use it correctly and know when not to trust it, not simply when the code ships.

The vault note reframes deployment as a governance transition rather than a technical milestone, because responsibility moves from the development team to operational stakeholders. That shift produces the deployment controls: approval gates contingent on compliance, legal and security signoffs; release procedures under which developers do not hold admin access to production; mandatory isolation between development, staging and production environments; and rollback procedures with verification steps, escalation contacts and fail-safe procedures. Deployment must be traceable, repeatable and reversible, which is what version control and a model registry deliver by recording versions, training-data lineage, deployment status and ownership.

The legal duties attach by role. Under the EU AI Act the deployer must use the system in accordance with the instructions, ensure input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose (Article 26), keep logs, monitor operation and report incidents to the provider. A deployer that substantially modifies a high-risk system becomes its provider, and the whole provider chain then applies.

The exam distinction: Deployment is the ISO phase and the governance transition; post-market monitoring under Article 72 is a separate, later provider duty.

term:Conformity Requirements.deep_dive:
Conformity requirements are the obligations an AI system must satisfy; conformity assessment is the procedure that demonstrates it. Exam items blur the two, so hold them apart: the requirement is what Article 15 demands of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity; the assessment is the Article 43 process that produces the evidence.

For a high-risk provider the chain runs in a fixed order, and the exam likes the sequence: complete the Chapter III requirements (risk management under Article 9, data governance under Article 10, technical documentation under Article 11, logging under Article 12, instructions for use under Article 13, human oversight under Article 14, accuracy and cybersecurity under Article 15, and the quality management system under Article 17), run the conformity assessment under Article 43, sign the EU declaration of conformity under Article 47, affix the CE marking under Article 48, and register in the EU database. Article 43 offers two routes: internal control under Annex VI, which is the default, or a notified-body review of the QMS and Annex IV documentation under Annex VII, which is compulsory for Annex III point 1 biometric systems unless the provider applies harmonised standards covering every relevant requirement. Article 40 gives a presumption of conformity where a harmonised standard's reference is published in the Official Journal.

Conformity requirements are not only regulatory. The vault note adds data provenance and licensing compliance, third-party audits or internal validation required by a governance board, and insurance-imposed requirements such as change management, code reviews and periodic risk assessments. A readiness gate that checks only the statute misses the obligations the organization's own contracts and insurers impose.
term:Conformity Requirements.exam_tip: Requirements versus assessment: Article 43 is the assessment procedure, and the chain runs assessment (43), declaration (47), CE marking (48), registration. Internal control is the Annex VI default; a notified body is mandatory for Annex III point 1 biometrics absent harmonised standards.

term:AI Partner.deep_dive:
This is ISO/IEC 22989 stakeholder vocabulary, and the definition is deliberately thin: a partner is an entity that collaborates in AI development or deployment. It sits in the same clause as AI provider (makes the system available), AI manufacturer (builds or assembles it), AI customer (acquires or uses it), AI subject (the individual affected by or interacting with it) and competent authorities. The vocabulary is descriptive rather than normative: 22989 tells you who is who, and other instruments attach duties to the roles they recognise.

That is the exam point. The BOK uses developer and deployer as task labels rather than legal categories, and the EU AI Act uses its own cast (provider, deployer, importer, distributor) with obligations attached to each. A partner in the ISO sense maps onto whichever of those the facts support. A cloud platform, a base-model vendor, a data supplier, a labelling vendor or a systems integrator can each be a partner, and each can also become a provider under the Act if it places a system on the market under its own name or substantially modifies one.

The practical consequence is third-party risk. Whatever the partner does becomes the deploying organization's exposure without its visibility: opaque training data, silently changing model versions, sub-tier suppliers, and contractual gaps around fairness, audit and incident response. The response is procurement intake that flags AI, AI-specific due diligence on training-data rights and model-change practices, and contracts carrying audit rights, incident notification and liability allocation.

The distinction the exam tests: a partner's collaboration never transfers the accountability that regulators and affected people place on the organization operating the system.
term:AI Partner.exam_tip: AI partner is ISO 22989 stakeholder vocabulary for a collaborator in development or deployment; it is descriptive, while provider and deployer are the AI Act's legal categories. Partner risk is third-party risk, and it never transfers your accountability.

term:A/B Testing.deep_dive:
A/B testing runs two variants of a model or system at the same time and compares outcomes, which makes it a deployment validation method rather than a development one. It sits with the staged release techniques the vault note lists: staged rollouts behind feature flags, and canary deployments that release to a small subset before full rollout. The governance value is that it tests the system under real conditions rather than in a test harness; the governance risk is the same, because users are exposed to a version that has not yet been accepted.

Three design decisions carry the weight. The comparison metric must be defined before the test, because a metric chosen after the results will flatter the preferred variant, and that is the same discipline as declaring accuracy metrics under Article 15. The split must be random and the subgroups must be checked separately, because a variant that wins on average can lose for a protected group, and a fairness finding hidden by an aggregate is exactly what the vault note's post-deployment bias monitoring exists to catch. The exposure must be bounded: an A/B test that runs on consequential decisions (credit, hiring, benefits) without a lawful basis or a documented risk assessment is a live experiment on people.

Where the test touches personal data, GDPR Article 22 is in play if the variant drives a decision with legal or similarly significant effects, and purpose limitation under Article 5(1)(b) limits reusing production data for experimentation beyond the stated purpose.

The exam distinction: A/B testing is a deployment validation control, and documenting the metric, the split and the decision is what turns it from an experiment into an evidential release step.
term:A/B Testing.exam_tip: A/B testing is deployment validation that exposes users to unaccepted variants, so define the metric in advance, check subgroups rather than the aggregate, and bound exposure. On consequential decisions it needs a lawful basis and an Article 22 analysis.

t_readiness.overview: Pre-release readiness is the gate between experimentation and production. It means documentation (the model card), conformity evidence (the EU AI Act conformity assessment for high-risk systems), operational testing (stress and failover), adversarial testing (red teaming), a pre-decided fail-safe, and a multidisciplinary review with named roles that formally signs off.
t_readiness.deep_dive:
### The readiness evaluation

A **production readiness evaluation** is a structured review covering safety, accountability, suitability for the intended context, regulatory conformity, performance benchmarking and operational planning. The **model card** is its headline artifact: a short document released with a trained model stating intended and out-of-scope uses, how it was evaluated, how it performs across relevant groups and conditions, and its known limitations. The format comes from Mitchell et al. (2019), and the exam's distinction is that a model card describes the model, a system card the whole deployed system, and a datasheet the dataset. Model cards also do governance work internally: writing one forces the team to confront assumptions, limitations and real-world performance rather than reporting a single accuracy figure.

### Conformity and legal obligations

For high-risk systems under the EU AI Act, release readiness includes a **conformity assessment** (Article 43), technical documentation under Article 11 and Annex IV, and the resulting EU declaration of conformity (Article 47) and CE marking (Article 48). Also required: evidence that all training and fine-tuning data was lawfully sourced, licensed and privacy-compliant; internal or third-party validation where governance boards demand it; and any insurance-imposed requirements, since cyber policies increasingly require change management, code review, gate reviews and periodic risk assessments.

### Operational and adversarial testing

**Stress testing** exercises the system under expected and edge-case workloads: latency and throughput benchmarks (critical for real-time use), memory and compute use under load, failover behaviour during outages or degraded performance, and evaluation against adversarial and malicious prompts. **Red teaming** is the adversarial complement: a team simulates attacks or misuse scenarios to surface vulnerabilities that standard testing misses, and it is the technique that catches prompt injection, jailbreaks, model extraction and misuse paths rather than ordinary bugs.

### Fail-safe and release mechanics

A **fail-safe plan** is a fallback decided in advance for when the system behaves anomalously, unsafely, or outside its set limits: halting safely, handing over to a backup system, or reverting to a manual process. The EU AI Act lists backup or fail-safe plans among the technical redundancy solutions supporting robustness of high-risk systems (Article 15(4); Recital 75). It is distinct from a **rollback procedure**, which reverses a release rather than the system's behaviour. Release itself runs through change management with release, verification and rollback procedures, then staged rollouts behind feature flags and canary deployments, monitoring for KPIs and leading risk indicators, and clear escalation channels.

### The final gate

Before release a multidisciplinary team confirms that documentation is complete (model cards, design artifacts, audit logs, licensing records, test reports), risk mitigations are implemented or deferrals approved, security hardening and incident response are validated, operational readiness and monitoring plans exist, compliance is verified, version control and traceability are intact, and users and operations staff are trained. Roles typically divide as legal (data use, licensing, contracts), engineering (technical validation and scalability), business (value alignment), cybersecurity (vulnerabilities addressed), privacy (data use review) and governance (fairness, accountability, transparency).
t_readiness.exam: Know which artifact does what: model card (the model), system card (the deployed system), datasheet (the dataset). Know the conformity chain for high-risk systems: conformity assessment under Article 43, technical documentation under Article 11 and Annex IV, declaration of conformity under Article 47, CE marking under Article 48. Expect the fail-safe against rollback distinction, and red teaming as the technique for misuse and attack scenarios rather than functional bugs. Readiness is a documented, multidisciplinary decision, not a benchmark score.

term:Stress Testing (AI).deep_dive:
The vault note defines the scope precisely: expected and edge-case workloads, latency and throughput benchmarks (especially for real-time use cases), memory and compute usage under load, failover behaviour during outages or degraded performance, and evaluation against adversarial and malicious prompts. The point of listing them together is that a model being accurate and a system holding up under load are different claims, and readiness needs both.

Stress testing is where the deployment mode decision gets validated. An edge deployment is chosen for low latency and offline operation, so its stress test must demonstrate behaviour when the network drops and when model size constraints bite; a cloud deployment's stress test must show graceful degradation when a dependency is slow rather than a cascade. Failover behaviour is the fail-safe plan under test: does the system reach its safe state, and does it do so within the time the risk assessment assumed.

The legal anchor is EU AI Act Article 15, which requires high-risk systems to achieve appropriate levels of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity throughout the life cycle and to be resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies. As amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI, Article 42(3) deems systems that meet the Cyber Resilience Regulation's requirements to satisfy the Article 15 cybersecurity limb. The NIST AI RMF Playbook expects the deployed system to be demonstrated to fail safely, particularly when pushed beyond its knowledge limits, with the range of conditions tested documented.

The exam distinction: stress testing is about behaviour under load and adverse conditions; red teaming is about an adversary choosing the input; both are pre-release controls and neither substitutes for the other.
term:Stress Testing (AI).exam_tip: Stress testing covers load, latency, resource use, failover and adversarial prompts; red teaming covers an attacker choosing inputs. Article 15 robustness and the Playbook wording that a system must be shown to fail safely are the anchors.

term:Red Teaming.deep_dive:
Red teaming is adversarial testing by design, and the governance question is what it adds over ordinary testing: it probes for the failures a cooperative test plan will not find, because the tester is trying to break the system rather than confirm it works. The vault note lists the AI-specific attack families a red team exercises: prompt injection and jailbreak testing against safety mechanisms, evasion attacks that flip a classification, poisoning of training or fine-tuning pipelines, functionality misuse where a legitimate tool is turned to an unintended end, and social engineering through a chatbot.

Scope matters. A credible red team covers the supporting infrastructure, APIs, integration layers and data pipelines, not just model weights, and it targets the people who build, manage and use the system as well as the system itself. Composition follows: domain experts who know the system, policy experts who know the misuse scenarios, and external testers who bring objectivity. MITRE ATLAS is the knowledge base that maps adversary tactics and techniques against AI, and NIST AI 100-2 is the taxonomy that separates poisoning, evasion, privacy and abuse attacks.

The legal hooks have hardened. For a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, presumed above 10^25 FLOP of cumulative training compute, Article 55 requires model evaluation including adversarial testing, documented and reported. Red teaming is also the canonical assurance technique for a pre-release readiness gate.

The exam distinction is purpose rather than method: red teaming finds vulnerabilities offensively, penetration testing validates the security controls, and ordinary validation testing confirms the system meets its requirements.
term:Red Teaming.exam_tip: Red teaming is offensive adversarial testing across the ecosystem, not just the model, and it is a named duty for systemic-risk GPAI under Article 55. Keep it distinct from validation testing (does it meet requirements) and penetration testing (are the controls effective).

term:Production Readiness Evaluation.deep_dive:
The readiness evaluation is the point where experimentation becomes operation, and its output is a governed go/no-go decision with named owners rather than a technical milestone. The vault note frames it as covering safety, accountability and suitability for the intended context, then lists the final gate review checks a multidisciplinary team runs: documentation complete (model cards, design artifacts, audit logs, licensing records, test reports), risk mitigations implemented or deferrals approved, security hardening and incident response validated, monitoring plans in place, compliance verified, version control and traceability maintained, and users trained.

Two formal reviews sit inside it. An AI impact assessment evaluates social, ethical and operational impact; a risk assessment articulates the harm events and their mitigations. Neither is optional in a mature programme, and the readiness verdict is technical and governance at once.

The legal overlay matters for high-risk systems. Conformity assessment under Article 43 must be complete before the system is placed on the market, which for an Annex III system means internal control under Annex VI or a notified-body review under Annex VII, followed by the Article 47 declaration and Article 48 CE marking. As amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027 and Annex I product-embedded systems from 2 August 2028, so a readiness gate built now is a rehearsal for those dates.

The distinction the exam tests: passing performance benchmarks is not readiness. A scenario that clears accuracy thresholds but lacks signoffs, a rollback procedure or a monitoring plan has failed the evaluation, not partly passed it.
term:Production Readiness Evaluation.exam_tip: Readiness is technical and governance together: documentation, risk mitigations, conformity, monitoring, rollback and signoffs. A system that clears performance benchmarks but has no rollback plan or approvals has not passed the gate.

term:Model Card.deep_dive:
Model cards were proposed by Mitchell et al. at FAT* 2019 as a short, standard disclosure that travels with a model. The BOK places creating one in release readiness, and the reason is governance rather than marketing: a card forces the team to state intended and out-of-scope uses, the evaluation data and metrics, results broken down by relevant groups and conditions, and known limitations. Writing down the out-of-scope uses is the part teams resist and the part a downstream deployer or a regulator most needs.

Keep the three documentation artifacts apart, because exam items swap them. A model card covers one model. A datasheet (Gebru et al., 2018) covers a dataset: its composition, collection process, uses and distribution. A system card covers the whole deployed system, including the non-model components, the integration and the operational context. A general-purpose AI provider's technical documentation and its public training-content summary under Article 53 are a separate statutory artifact set that overlaps the model card without replacing it.

The practical consequence is inheritance. Where a system is built on someone else's base model, the card is often the only window into the training data, the data rights and the evaluation, which is why NIST AI 600-1 treats value-chain and component integration as a generative-AI risk. A card that omits limitations converts an unknown into an assumption.

Under ISO/IEC 42001 the card is documented information the AI management system maintains, and under the EU AI Act's technical documentation duty the underlying facts must exist whether or not a card is published. The exam distinction is artifact scope: one model, one dataset, or one assembled system.

term:Fail-Safe Plan.deep_dive:
The legal anchor is EU AI Act Article 15(4), which requires high-risk systems to be resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies and names backup or fail-safe plans among the technical redundancy solutions that support robustness. Recital 75 supplies the purpose: a fail-safe mechanism is what lets a system safely interrupt its operation rather than continue down a harmful path.

The design work is deciding what safe means here, because halting is not automatically safe. A clinical decision support tool fails safe by handing the case back to the clinician; a vehicle or an industrial controller that stops abruptly may create a worse hazard, so its fail-safe is a controlled minimal-risk state. An agentic system fails safe by denying an action by default when the approval service is unavailable, which is fail-closed; a timeout that lets the action proceed when nobody answers is fail-open, and fail-open is the wrong default for anything consequential.

A usable plan names four things: the triggers (anomalous output, out-of-bounds input, lost sensor or data feed, repeated human override), the safe state, the person authorised to invoke it, and the evidence that it was tested. Without the last item the plan is an assertion rather than a control.

Three distinctions the exam tests. Fail-safe is the pre-decided fallback; human oversight under Article 14 is the ability to understand, override and interrupt during normal operation; a deactivation policy is the governed decision to retire a system. Article 15(4) files fail-safe and technical redundancy under robustness, not under accuracy, cybersecurity or human oversight, so an option that places the fail-safe plan in the cybersecurity bucket is the distractor.
term:Fail-Safe Plan.exam_tip: Article 15(4) puts backup and fail-safe plans under robustness and technical redundancy, not accuracy or cybersecurity. The exam distinction is fail-safe (automatic fallback to a safe state) versus Article 14 oversight (human override) versus deactivation (governed retirement).

ch9.overview: III.B governs data and the evidence it produces: a defendable legal right to collect and use the data, quality judged against defined dimensions, fitness for the intended purpose, lineage and provenance records, and a testing regime that goes well past accuracy to cover integration, performance, security, bias and interpretability, with the risks each test is meant to catch.
ch9.deep_dive:
III.B carries 6 to 8 questions and is the most technical of the three competencies, but its questions are governance questions wearing technical clothes.

### 1. Data governance

The first step is not quality, it is **authority**: a formally verified, defendable legal right to collect, process, store and analyse the data. Bases include direct consent, contract, privacy notice, or a regulatory allowance (HIPAA-compliant sharing with deidentification and a business associate agreement). Watch for **secondary use**: repurposing data beyond its collection purpose is function creep and needs a compatibility assessment or a fresh basis. Quality is judged on dimensions rather than a feeling: accuracy, completeness, integrity across datasets, timeliness, consistency. Sufficiency (enough volume) and representativeness (captures the diversity of the deployment environment) are separate questions, and the two classic failures are opposite ends of one dial: too little data underfits, too much narrow or repetitive data overfits. Fitness for purpose is a governance judgement, and the exam's hook is that technically similar data carries very different exposure: a translation corpus is not a medical advice corpus.

Roles: **data stewards** are operational custodians for quality, documentation and issue resolution; Security sits at the data layer (encryption, access management, audit logging on training data) and the infrastructure layer. ### 2. Lineage and provenance

The distinction the exam returns to: **provenance** looks backward to origin (where it came from, who created it, under what conditions, with what licence and intended purpose), while **lineage** tracks flow forward through ingestion, storage, transformation, consumption, maintenance and disposal. Provenance starts with metadata: source entity, collection method and date, version, licence, access rights, intended use, jurisdiction, and the assumptions and limitations attached.

Failure modes are organizational more than technical: departmental silos where datasets move without clear ownership, **shadow AI** development outside sanctioned pipelines, and fragmented manual documentation. ### 3. Testing and the risks it catches

AI testing differs from ordinary software testing because behaviour is learned, stochastic and data-dependent. The suite: **unit and component testing** on transformations, wrappers and scoring functions; **integration testing** across ingestion, inference, storage and downstream systems, including failure conditions; **validation testing** against the stated business problem, with criteria defined before testing starts; **performance testing** for latency, throughput and resource use, and specifically for the peak rather than the average; **security testing** for adversarial inputs, poisoning and backdoors, model extraction and inversion, plus conventional scans and penetration tests; **bias and fairness testing** for performance parity across groups and counterfactual fairness; and **interpretability testing** with model-agnostic tools (SHAP, LIME), global feature importance, and simulatability.

Each test maps to a risk it exists to catch. Data-related: biased or unrepresentative training data, label noise, outliers, imbalanced classes, concept drift. Model-related: overfitting, underfitting, brittleness on edge cases, poor calibration. Evaluation-related: the wrong metric, test set leakage, insufficient subgroup coverage. Deployment-related: environment mismatch, shadow AI, feedback loops, new attack surfaces in production.

Mitigations are data augmentation, resampling, carefully constructed synthetic data, regularization (L1, L2, dropout) for overfitting, and ensembles. Testing is documented as a plan (objectives, scope, scenarios, metrics, pass/fail criteria) and as results (issues, remediation, after-action review, dataset and code versions), and regression tested whenever operating parameters or training data change.
ch9.exam: Six to eight questions. The single most reliable distinction is lineage against provenance: provenance is origin and terms, lineage is the transformation trail. Next is data quality against data sufficiency against representativeness, which are three different assessments. Then the testing suite: expect a stem describing a failure (the model collapses on slightly-off inputs, or accuracy is high but one subgroup fails) and asking which test or risk type it illustrates. Remember that an aggregate accuracy figure routinely hides subgroup failure, and that a validation set score does not survive dataset shift. Under the EU AI Act, Article 10 requires training, validation and testing datasets to be relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete.
key_points: Lawful authority to use the data comes before data quality; internal data is not automatically usable data
Secondary use is function creep: repurposing training data beyond its collection purpose needs a compatibility assessment or a fresh basis
Data quality dimensions: accuracy, completeness, integrity, timeliness, consistency; sufficiency and representativeness are separate questions
Underfitting comes from too little data, overfitting from too much narrow or repetitive data
Provenance looks backward to origin and terms; lineage tracks forward through transformation, consumption and disposal

t_train.overview: Training data and methods decide what a model can learn. This topic covers how data is labeled and what ground truth means, the two failure modes at either end of the data-volume dial (underfitting and overfitting), the techniques used to build or stretch a dataset (synthetic data, RLHF), the evaluation set held back from training, and the transparency obligations that document what went in.
t_train.deep_dive:
### Labels, annotation and ground truth

**Data annotation** attaches descriptive information to data without altering the data itself, and in supervised learning it is the label the model is trained to predict. Its quality control is inter-rater reliability: a measure of agreement among labelers, which is the practical defence against label noise. **Ground truth** is the value of the target variable for a specific labeled element, and the governance point is that ground truth is not automatically true. If the label encodes a human judgement made under bad conditions, or a proxy that does not measure what you think, the model learns that error faithfully. Annotation guidelines, labeler training, disagreement resolution and documented label provenance are therefore governance controls, not housekeeping.

**Named entity recognition** is the task of recognizing and labeling the names of entities and their categories across sequences of words. ### Underfitting and overfitting

**Underfitting** is a model too simple, or trained on too little data, to capture the underlying patterns, so it performs poorly on training data and new data alike. **Overfitting** is the opposite: the model learns the training data too precisely, including its noise, and fails to generalize. The governance framing is that these are data-volume and data-diversity problems before they are hyperparameter problems, which is why sufficiency thresholds and reuse limits belong in policy. Mitigations for overfitting include **regularization** (L1 adds a penalty on the absolute value of parameters and simplifies the model, L2 penalizes the square of parameters and promotes stability, dropout does the equivalent in neural networks), more and more varied data, and **ensembles** or model stacking, which cover the weaknesses of any single approach. The diagnostic habit worth carrying into the exam: poor performance on both training and test data suggests underfitting, good training performance with poor test performance suggests overfitting.

### Synthetic data and RLHF

**Synthetic data** is artificially generated records that imitate the patterns and statistical make-up of a real dataset without copying actual records. It is used where real data is scarce, skewed toward some groups, or too risky to use or share, and it is a legitimate representativeness remedy. It lowers but does not remove privacy risk, because a generator trained on personal data can reproduce details of real people, so the governance requirement is to verify that synthetic records cannot be reidentified. **Reinforcement learning with human feedback** is a training technique in which people compare or rank a model's outputs, a reward model is trained on those preferences, and reinforcement learning then tunes the model toward the responses people prefer. It is how chat-style language models are steered toward helpful, harmless answers, and it inherits its own bias risks: the annotator pool's preferences become the model's disposition, and the ranking task is labour-intensive and hard to audit.

### Test data and transparency

**Test data** (evaluation data) is held back from training and used to evaluate the final model, and it is distinct from both training data and validation data. Overlap between training and test data is **test set leakage**, which inflates performance and is one of the named evaluation risks. Transparency is the last piece: ISO/IEC 22989 defines system transparency as appropriate information about the system being made available to relevant interested parties, which may include characteristics, performance, limitations, components, procedures, measures, design objectives, data sources and labeling protocols. That list is effectively a description of training documentation, which is why the training process and the transparency obligation are the same evidence viewed from two directions.
t_train.exam: The pair to hold onto is underfitting against overfitting, with the diagnostic being training-set performance: weak on both means underfitting, strong on training and weak on test means overfitting. Know L1, L2 and dropout as regularization, and ensembles as a general mitigation. Test data is held back; overlap with training data is leakage. Synthetic data reduces but does not remove privacy risk, and RLHF tunes a model toward annotator preferences, so it inherits their biases.

Regularization: L1 simplifies, L2 stabilizes, dropout does the equivalent in neural networks; ensembles cover single-model weaknesses

term:Underfitting.deep_dive:
Underfitting is the model that never learned: too simple, too constrained, or trained on too little data to capture the patterns in the problem, so it performs poorly on the training data and on new data alike. The vault note gives the governance cause directly, **insufficient volume of training data**, which makes underfitting the mirror image of overfitting: one is fed too much narrow data and memorises, the other is fed too little and never generalises.

The remedies run opposite to overfitting's, which is why the pair is worth learning together. Where overfitting calls for regularization, dropout, early stopping and simpler models, underfitting calls for more capacity, richer features, longer training and, most often, more data. In a governance scenario the last of those is the interesting one, because data volume and representativeness are the subject of the data governance requirements rather than a modelling preference.

The hooks are therefore about data sufficiency. EU AI Act Article 10 requires high-risk datasets to be relevant, sufficiently representative and as complete as possible for the intended purpose, which is a legal statement of what underfitting exposes as absent. NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.5 requires the deployed system to be demonstrated valid and reliable with documented limits on generalisability, and MEASURE 2.3 requires performance to be demonstrated under conditions similar to the deployment setting, which catches a model that looks adequate only because it was assessed in a narrow setting.

The exam distinction is the diagnostic pair: bad on training and bad on new data means underfitting, good on training and bad on new data means overfitting. Reading the symptom correctly points to the right remedy, and choosing the wrong one makes the problem worse, since regularizing an underfit model or adding capacity to an overfit one moves it further from the right balance.
term:Underfitting.exam_tip: Underfitting is poor performance everywhere because the model or the data volume is insufficient, usually caused by too little training data. Read it against overfitting: bad everywhere versus bad only on new data.

term:Transparency (System).deep_dive:
Transparency is a property of a system whereby appropriate information about it is made available to relevant interested parties. ISO/IEC 22989 gives a concrete list of what that information may cover: characteristics, performance, limitations, components, procedures, measures, design objectives, data sources and labelling protocols. Read as a checklist, that list is close to what a technical file contains.

Three distinctions do the exam work. **Transparency versus explainability**: transparency is the availability of information about the system; explainability is the property that lets important factors behind a specific result be expressed understandably, answering why a particular output came out as it did. One is documentation, the other is comprehension of an instance. **System versus organisation**: ISO defines a separate term, transparency of an organisation, for communicating activities and decisions comprehensively and accessibly, so the two are not interchangeable. And **disclosure has limits**: the standard itself notes that inappropriate disclosure can violate security or privacy, which is why transparency is calibrated to the audience rather than maximised.

The legal hooks give it teeth. EU AI Act Article 13 requires high-risk systems to operate transparently enough for deployers to interpret output, with instructions for use covering capabilities, limitations, accuracy and robustness metrics, known risks and human oversight measures. Article 11 requires technical documentation per Annex IV before market placement. Article 50 imposes transparency duties toward users for certain systems and generated content. In data protection law the same logic appears in GDPR Articles 13 and 14, and the ICO guidance on explaining decisions made with AI ties it to meaningful information about the logic involved. NIST pairs the characteristic as **accountable and transparent** and treats it as cross-cutting.

The exam distinction: transparency supplies information, explainability makes outputs comprehensible, and neither requires giving up trade secrets or personal data.
term:Transparency (System).exam_tip: Transparency is information availability about the system; explainability is comprehensibility of a specific output. Article 13 is the high-risk hook, and ISO warns that inappropriate disclosure can breach security or privacy.

term:Test Data (Evaluation Data).deep_dive:
Test data is the held-out exam: data used to evaluate the performance of a final model, distinct from training data and validation data. ISO/IEC 22989 draws the line precisely. Training data fits the model, validation data compares candidate models and tunes hyperparameters, and test data estimates performance once. The integrity of that separation is what makes the number mean anything.

Two corruptions destroy it. **Test-set leakage**, where records appear in both training and test sets, means the model has already seen its exam and the reported performance is inflated. **Repeated tuning against the test set** has the same effect gradually, because each iteration leaks information from the test set back into the model and turns evaluation into training. Both are governance failures, not measurement quirks, because every downstream claim, from accuracy to bias metrics, rests on this set.

The legal and framework hooks are specific. EU AI Act Article 10 requires training, validation and testing datasets for high-risk systems to be relevant, representative, as free of errors as possible and complete, and to be examined for bias, which presupposes documented, distinguishable sets. NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.1 requires test sets, metrics and the tools used during testing, evaluation, verification and validation to be documented. NIST AI 600-1 warns that label errors in test datasets destabilise benchmarks used for model selection, so test data quality affects which model is chosen.

The coverage point completes it. A test set that omits a subgroup or a production use case reports a performance the system does not have, which is why the vault note lists insufficient coverage as an evaluation risk. The exam distinction: test data is used once, at the end, and any scenario that tunes against it or mixes it with training data has invalidated the results.
term:Test Data (Evaluation Data).exam_tip: Test data evaluates the final model once, after training and validation. Leakage or tuning against it converts evaluation into training and inflates every metric, and coverage gaps hide subgroup failures.

term:Synthetic Data.deep_dive:
Synthetic data is artificially generated data that imitates the patterns and statistical make-up of a real dataset without copying its records. It is used where genuine data is scarce, skewed toward some groups, or too risky to use or share, and it is a data-preparation technique: ISO/IEC 22989 defines data augmentation as creating synthetic samples by modifying or utilising existing data, which is the same family of methods.

It is genuinely useful in governance terms. Synthetic data can supply the under-represented group in an imbalanced dataset, which is a fairness intervention, and it can reduce the exposure of personal data by training on generated records instead of real ones. The GDPR guidance in the vault note treats synthetic data generation as a minimisation technique, and lists it among the options to consider before scraping or reusing personal data.

The limits are where the exam sits. **Synthetic does not mean non-personal.** A generator trained on personal data can memorise and reproduce details of real people, which is the mechanism behind membership inference and extraction attacks on generative models, so synthetic records can still be personal data and the generation step is itself processing. **It can degrade the model.** NIST AI 600-1 describes model collapse: over-reliance on synthetic data causes data points to disappear from the output distribution, so a model trained on its own descendants narrows rather than generalises.

The legal hooks are explicit. EU AI Act Article 10(5) as enacted contemplated synthetic or augmented data where real data is insufficient, subject to the quality requirements and a check that no bias is introduced, and Article 4a, added by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), names synthetic or anonymised data as the first thing to try before processing special category data for bias detection, under the safeguard of no effective alternative.

The exam distinction: synthetic data lowers privacy risk, it does not eliminate it, and it must be validated for representativeness rather than assumed representative.
term:Synthetic Data.exam_tip: Synthetic data helps with scarcity, imbalance and privacy, but a generator can reproduce real people and over-reliance causes model collapse. Article 4a treats it as the alternative to try first before processing special category data.
