term:Data Quality.deep_dive:
The vault note's dimensions are the ones to name: accuracy (values correct and free from error), completeness (required fields populated), integrity (relationships across datasets correctly maintained), timeliness (up to date) and consistency (values follow expected formats and rules). Add representativeness, which is where quality stops being hygiene and becomes a fairness question.

### Quality is always relative to purpose

The note's key insight is that a dataset for language translation may not be suitable for training a medical advice chatbot, even though the data is technically similar. Fitness for purpose includes regulatory compliance, integration with workflows and suitability for the operational environment, so the same dataset can pass one use and fail another. This is why the exam can hand you a dataset that is clean, complete and lawfully collected and still ask what is wrong: nothing, for the wrong purpose.

### The statutory floor

Article 10(3) requires high-risk training, validation and testing datasets to be relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete for the intended purpose, with attention to the statistical properties of the persons or groups on whom the system will be used. Article 10(2)(g) adds examination for possible biases. The note's own warning about accuracy metrics is worth keeping in mind: in a condition with 5% prevalence, a 95%-accurate diagnostic model may be labelling almost everyone healthy.

### The failure modes

The note's testing-risk table doubles as a quality checklist: biased training data, label noise, outliers and anomalies, imbalanced datasets, concept drift, and test set leakage. Quality failures are usually silent, which is why they surface as performance or fairness incidents rather than as build errors.

### The distinction

Data quality is not data integrity (integrity is one dimension of it) and not data sufficiency (enough volume). Accuracy is per-field correctness; quality is a property of the dataset measured against a purpose. NIST SP 1270 shows how collection and preparation choices turn into systemic bias.
term:Data Quality.exam_tip: Quality is relative to purpose: a clean, complete, lawfully collected dataset can still be unfit for the intended use. Name the dimensions (accuracy, completeness, integrity, timeliness, consistency, representativeness) and cite Article 10(3) for high-risk datasets.

term:Data Poisoning.deep_dive:
The vocabulary matters more than the mechanism here, because the exam tests the attack class. NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy (AI 100-2) sorts attacks by the attacker's goal and the stage: poisoning is an **integrity** attack at training time, evasion is an integrity attack at inference time, and extraction or inference attacks are **confidentiality** attacks on the model. Poisoning splits again into availability poisoning, which degrades overall performance, and targeted poisoning, which installs a **backdoor** that fires only when a trigger pattern appears. A backdoored model can score normally on ordinary test sets, which is why accuracy testing is not a poisoning defence.

### The realistic vectors

Scraped web content (an attacker registers domains likely to be crawled), crowdsourced or outsourced labelling, third-party and open datasets, and fine-tuning data supplied by users. OWASP's Top 10 for LLM applications lists the generative version as data and model poisoning and pairs it with supply-chain risk, since a poisoned pretrained model arrives already compromised.

### What defends

The controls are upstream: provenance and source vetting, integrity hashing and version control of datasets, anomaly and outlier detection in training data, label-quality review, data sanitisation, and targeted trigger testing. The vault note places this under security testing for AI, alongside backdoor assessment, and names the absence of provenance as what conceals tampering.

### The legal hooks

EU AI Act Article 15(5) lists data poisoning among the AI-specific vulnerabilities a high-risk system must be resilient to where appropriate, and Article 15(4) requires the testing that evidences it; Article 9 requires the risk to be managed across the lifecycle; Article 10(3) supplies the data-quality duties that shrink the surface. For a GPAI model with systemic risk, Article 55 requires documented adversarial evaluation. Because the model may pass ordinary validation, the governance answer is provenance plus integrity controls rather than a test score.

### The exam distinction

Timing is the tell. Poisoning acts on the training data before deployment; evasion and prompt injection act on inputs at inference; model inversion and membership inference extract information from the model. Article 15(5) is the article to cite.
term:Data Poisoning.exam_tip: Poisoning is a training-time integrity attack; evasion and prompt injection are inference-time; inversion and membership inference are confidentiality attacks. Availability poisoning degrades performance, targeted poisoning installs a trigger-locked backdoor, and Article 15(5) is the AI Act hook.

term:Data Governance.deep_dive:
The vault note's framing is that AI systems are only as reliable as the data they are trained on, so data governance is an enabler and even a prerequisite of responsible AI development. That is why the EU AI Act lifts it into law: Article 10(1) makes data governance a high-risk provider obligation, and Article 10(2) spells out what it covers.

### What Article 10(2) actually requires

It covers design choices, data collection processes and origin, preparation operations (annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment, aggregation), assumptions about what the data measures and represents, examination for possible biases, identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings, and the measures taken to address them. The practical consequence is that a policy document cannot satisfy Article 10: the assumptions and the gap analysis have to be written down.

### The components the note names

The note's governance toolkit is classification (risk levels with handling rules), data flow diagrams, input and output controls (data entering or leaving a system is approved and correctly formatted), and data loss prevention. It also fixes the role split that exam items test: **data stewards** are operational custodians who keep quality, documentation and issue resolution under control, while **data owners** are accountable for strategic use, approve use cases, certify lawful use and sign off on risk assessments.

### Where it sits in the management system

Article 17 requires a quality management system, and data governance is one of the processes it must document and control; ISO/IEC 42001 provides the certifiable management-system frame, and the note points to ISO/IEC 38505-1 for data governance specifically. Governance is a lifecycle process; the maturity ladder runs ad hoc, emerging, defined, managed, optimized.

### The pitfalls the exam uses

Treating governance as compliance (ticking boxes), overcentralization, tool overload, and shadow copies of training data pulled from production for ad hoc filtering without recording the procedure. The note also mandates privacy impact assessments for any AI system processing personal data.

### The distinction

Governance is the framework of policies, roles and controls; a privacy impact assessment is one artifact produced under it, and a data-quality metric is a measurement taken inside it. The exam tests whether you can tell the framework from the artifact.
term:Data Governance.exam_tip: Data governance is the framework (policies, roles, controls), and Article 10(2) makes its artifacts mandatory for high-risk systems: assumptions, bias examination and data-gap analysis all in writing. Know data owner (accountable, certifies lawful use) versus data steward (operational custodian).

term:Data Acquisition.deep_dive:
Data acquisition is the gate, not the tap. The vault note puts the first step bluntly: before any data is collected for training, the organization must confirm a **defendable legal right** to collect, process, store and analyse it, and it treats a formal legal counsel review with a written assertion as essential rather than optional.

### The bases that count

The note's table of lawful bases is the examinable part, because two entries are traps. Direct consent (a checkbox), contractual provisions and privacy-policy declarations are the ordinary bases. **Implicit consent** is the trap: the note states it is insufficient in some jurisdictions, including the EU under the GDPR, where Article 6 requires a real lawful basis and Article 5(1)(b) limits use to the purpose the data was collected for. Regulatory allowances are the other special case: HIPAA-compliant health data sharing usually requires de-identification and a Business Associate Agreement.

### What acquisition must produce

The note requires the acquisition record to carry data source registration, consent records, contract references, privacy-policy references and jurisdiction-specific legal justifications. That record is what later answers an audit. Where the source is a third party, the note wants contractual terms that forbid use of the training data for any other system, customer or purpose, plus a right to audit, third-party security assessment, termination without cause and destruction of data on request.

### The two failure modes

**Function creep** is the first: repurposing data beyond its original collection purpose, which the note ties directly to privacy-policy, contract and regulatory violations. **Silent acquisition** is the second: data pulled from a source whose terms nobody read, including scraped web content. For scraped material the relevant lever is Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790, the text and data mining exception, which a rights-holder can reserve; the EU AI Act then makes GPAI providers honour those reservations through a copyright policy under Article 53(1)(c).

### The exam distinction

Possessing data is not the same as having the right to train on it. Acquisition is where rights are checked, and most training-data legal problems are acquisition problems discovered too late. Article 10(2) of the EU AI Act makes collection processes and the origin of the data a documented high-risk obligation.
term:Data Acquisition.exam_tip: Possession is not a right to train: the tested control is the acquisition-stage rights check, with a written legal assertion and a jurisdiction-specific justification on file. Implicit consent is the trap answer, because the GDPR does not accept it as a lawful basis.

ch8.overview: III.A governs the front of the lifecycle: framing the business context and the use case, running an impact assessment, applying policy, procedure and ethics to the design itself (purpose, requirements, architecture and model selection, human oversight, metrics and thresholds, stakeholder feedback, operational controls), identifying and managing internal and external design risk, and documenting all of it.
ch8.deep_dive:
III.A carries 6 to 8 questions and is five indicators, mapping onto the knowledge area's sections almost one to one.

### 1. Business context and use case

Settle these before requirements are frozen. The business context is the organizational, strategic and operational environment the system sits in; the use case turns it into a specification covering intended function, users and environments, assumptions and constraints, decision authority, and expected lifetime and workload. Success metrics are named up front, and the classic trap is optimizing one at another's expense: pushing precision up raises false negatives, chasing efficiency can cost transparency. ### 2. Impact assessment

An AI impact assessment identifies and manages harms and unintended consequences before deployment. Scope it (system, uses, affected populations, jurisdictions, autonomy level), assemble the inputs (design artifacts, applicable law, data flows, performance metrics, prior incidents), then work through impacts, likelihood, severity, scope and reversibility. Two easy errors: discrimination survives the removal of protected attributes through proxies, so assess **outcomes** not features; and human oversight is real only if the reviewer has time, authority, visibility and a documented escalation path. ### 3. Policy, procedure, best practice and ethics applied to design

Design begins by asking whether AI is the right tool and what the unintended outcomes might be, then works through architecture and model selection. Modularity pays off later: separate ingestion, inference and output rendering so each can be tested alone, and log state transitions for auditability. Model choice is a tradeoff set, not a leaderboard: accuracy against interpretability, speed against cost, personalization against fairness, data volume against privacy and attack surface. High-stakes decisions often want the simpler, explainable model.

Human oversight is designed as approver, reviewer or escalation point, with plain-language explanations and overrides logged with a rationale. Metrics and thresholds are governance decisions: where the threshold sits decides who bears which error, so threshold changes need approval and a recorded rationale. Operational controls are the AI-specific additions: anomaly alerting, failsafe defaults, shadow-mode deployment, and a kill switch.

### 4. Internal and external design risk

AI adds nondeterminism, opacity and emergent behaviour to ordinary software risk. Internal risks sit inside the organization's control: faulty assumptions, inadequate documentation, poor or insufficient training data, integration failures, incomplete testing, missing explainability, no monitoring. External risks largely do not: adversarial use, legal and regulatory change, supply chain compromise, cultural backlash, user misuse. The named techniques: a **probability/severity matrix** to score and prioritize; a **risk mitigation hierarchy** running eliminate, substitute, engineer safeguards, warn and train, accept with monitoring; **stakeholder mapping**, because users, subjects, operators, regulators and the public perceive risk differently; and **benchmarking**, which also helps defend the decision later. ### 5. Documentation

A design baseline records purpose and scope, stakeholders and roles, ethical and regulatory considerations, system boundaries and interfaces, data and model design, and risk and lifecycle management. ### 6. Proprietary models

An organization that develops and deploys its own model owns the whole chain: data legality, performance and fairness, transparency, post-deployment behaviour and disposal. Under the EU AI Act it is the **provider**, not merely the deployer, which shifts conformity assessment, technical documentation, logging, quality management, human oversight and incident reporting onto it.
ch8.exam: Six to eight questions. The BOK lists the indicator contents explicitly (purpose, requirements gathering, architecture and model selection, human oversight, data analysis, metric and threshold evaluation, stakeholder engagement and feedback, operational controls), so a stem naming one of those is asking which control or artifact belongs there. Two recurring distinctions: an organization that builds its own model is the provider and carries upstream duties, and a threshold is a value judgment about who bears which error rather than a tuning parameter. Expect one question on the risk mitigation hierarchy's order, and one on why removing protected attributes does not remove discrimination.

t_impact.overview: An AI impact assessment identifies and manages the harms, benefits and unintended consequences of a system before deployment, and again whenever the system, its use or its context changes. ISO/IEC 42005 is the method; ISO/IEC 42001 requires the assessment; the EU AI Act requires a fundamental rights impact assessment for certain deployers. It is a lifecycle activity, not a one-off gate.
t_impact.deep_dive:
### What it is, and what it is not

An AI impact assessment looks outward at the people and societies the system can affect. That is the distinction from ISO/IEC 23894, which manages risk to the organization's own objectives; the two feed each other, and ISO/IEC 42005's Annex B explains how. It is also **guidance, not a requirements standard**: nothing is certified to 42005. ISO/IEC 42001 is the certifiable management system, and it requires an impact assessment at clauses 6.1.4 and 8.4 and Annex A objective A.5, which is the gap 42005 fills.

### The record

A complete assessment records scope (system, version, uses); AI system information including intended and unintended uses; data sources, characteristics and quality; algorithms and how models were developed; the deployment environment (geography, languages, constraints); relevant interested parties, split into directly affected and other parties; **actual and reasonably foreseeable impacts**, covering benefits as well as harms, failure modes and reasonably foreseeable misuse; and the measures that address them. A record with no benefits, no unintended uses or no misuse analysis is incomplete, and that is a common exam trap.

### Timing and triggers

Assess at design, while changes are still cheap; before deployment, as a release gate; during operation through monitoring and periodic review; and on significant change. The reassessment triggers are a change of intended use or purpose, a significant change to the system (new data types, retraining, a replaced model), a change in the legal or policy environment, and new evidence from monitoring or feedback. The demand-forecasting model quietly repurposed to rate individual workers is the standard illustration.

### The process, in order

ISO/IEC 42005's clause 5 is a documented process set up before any single system is assessed: write it down (procedure and templates), integrate it with enterprise risk, compliance, privacy and the AIMS rather than running it stand-alone, decide the timing, define the scope, assign responsibilities, set the thresholds and impact scales that decide depth and escalation, then perform, analyse, record and report, approve formally, and monitor and review. Sensitive and restricted uses are flagged by those thresholds and get escalation and formal approval.

### Legal drivers

The EU AI Act requires a **fundamental rights impact assessment** for deployers of certain high-risk systems (Article 27), on top of the provider's risk management system under Article 9. Canada's DADM requires algorithmic impact assessments for automated decision-making, California's privacy regime gives the regulator power to require risk assessments for automated decision-making, and the OECD and G7 treat impact assessment as best practice. Sector and privacy assessments overlap but are not substitutes: a GDPR DPIA covers data protection risk, not the full impact picture.

### Making it count

An assessment is only worth the change it causes. Findings must feed model features, training data, interfaces, rollout plans and monitoring; they should be reviewed by someone with governance authority (legal, risk, ethics, and executive or board endorsement for high-risk systems); risk acceptance is recorded with the name of whoever accepted it, along with residual risk and the tradeoffs accepted; and publication is deliberate, since public summaries build trust while proprietary architectures and protected data should stay out.
t_impact.exam: The highest-yield facts: ISO/IEC 42005 is guidance and cannot be certified; ISO/IEC 42001 is what requires an impact assessment; and 42005 looks at impacts on people while 23894 looks at risk to the organization. Expect a question about when to reassess (significant change, new data, new regulation, monitoring findings) and one about what belongs in the record, where the trap is omitting benefits, unintended uses or foreseeable misuse. The EU AI Act's deployer-side Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment is distinct from the provider's Article 9 risk management system.

term:Impact Assessment.deep_dive:
An impact assessment is the structured attempt to see the consequences of a system before deployment, and the exam rewards knowing which instrument is which. **ISO/IEC 42005:2025**, published 28 May 2025, is the guidance standard for AI system impact assessment. It is **not certifiable**: no one holds a 42005 certificate. What is certifiable is **ISO/IEC 42001:2023**, which *requires* an impact assessment (Clause 6.1.4 in planning, Clause 8.4 in operation, and Annex A objective A.5) and says little about how to do one. 42005 fills that gap, and its Annex A maps the two.

The lens matters. **ISO/IEC 23894** asks what could stop the organization meeting its objectives: risk to the business. **ISO/IEC 42005** asks how the system could affect individuals, groups and societies, for better or worse. A 42005 record must contain **benefits as well as harms**, and **actual and reasonably foreseeable impacts** including failures and foreseeable misuse. A record with no benefits and no misuse section is incomplete.

Legally, three duties are separate and none is satisfied by a voluntary standard. **GDPR Article 35** requires a data protection impact assessment where processing is likely to result in high risk. **EU AI Act Article 27** requires a fundamental rights impact assessment from certain deployers (bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of the Annex III creditworthiness and life or health insurance pricing systems), before first use. **Article 9** requires a continuous risk management system for high-risk systems. One well-built 42005 record can feed both the DPIA and the FRIA, and the Omnibus amendment lets a deployer cross-reference DPIA sections in the FRIA, but neither law accepts the voluntary standard in place of its own assessment.
term:Impact Assessment.exam_tip: 42005 is guidance and cannot be certified; 42001 requires the assessment and is the certifiable standard. 42005 weighs benefits and harms for people, while 23894 manages risk to the organization. It can feed a GDPR Art. 35 DPIA or an AI Act Art. 27 FRIA but never replaces them.

t_usecase.overview: Governance starts here. The business context and the use case are formal deliverables completed before requirements are frozen: what problem the system solves, for whom, under what conditions, with what decision authority, measured how, and whether the organization can actually operate it. A misframed problem produces a well-built system that solves the wrong thing, and no amount of later testing repairs that.
t_usecase.deep_dive:
### What the use case has to contain

The business context is the organizational, strategic and operational environment: which objective the system supports, the expected business benefit, and organizational readiness (leadership commitment, data governance maturity, security and privacy maturity, risk culture, and cross-functional expertise across legal, IT, data science, operations, cybersecurity and privacy).

The use case then specifies the system: intended function (classification, prediction, assistance, recommendation), intended users and environments, assumptions and constraints, decision authority (autonomous or human in the loop), and expected lifetime, workload and frequency. Explicit boundaries are what prevent scope creep and unmanageable risk.

### Success metrics are a governance choice

Metrics are named up front and aligned to the business goal, and the exam's angle is that they conflict. Optimizing precision raises false negatives; optimizing efficiency can cost transparency; optimizing engagement can reward addiction loops. Fraud detection is measured on undetected fraud and false positive rate; a support chatbot on resolution time, escalation rate and satisfaction; a hiring tool on quality of hire, time to fill and bias across protected classes. Choosing the metric is choosing which harm you accept.

### Data availability and suitability

More AI projects fail on data than on models. Inventory what exists, where it lives and how it was collected; check completeness, accuracy, consistency and label availability; then check legal and ethical usability. Data can be technically perfect and still off limits: collected for another purpose (GDPR Article 5(1)(b) purpose limitation), carrying sensitive attributes, or supporting inferences the subject never expected. Readiness also means the pipeline can sustain the system, taking new data over time, serving real-time inference if needed, monitored for drift, and compliant with privacy and access controls on an ongoing basis.

### Ethical and operational red flags

Feasibility and value do not settle ethics. Watch high-stakes domains (criminal justice, housing, hiring, education, credit), reinforcement of historical bias, opacity in consequential decisions, and manipulation. Decision rights are part of the design: what may the system decide alone, when must a human be involved, how are overrides and appeals handled, is the oversight role resourced, and are there enough business records to defend the decision. Workforce readiness matters too, since workflows, roles and morale all move. A system can also be legal and profitable and still not fit the organization's public commitments, which is a reputational question rather than a compliance one.

### Use case assessment

A **use case assessment** is the pre-development gate: does this application fit organizational policy, risk appetite and ethical standards? Rigour scales with the use case. The test is decision impact, user exposure (internal or external), affected rights or opportunities, automation level, applicable regulation, and context such as cultural norms or prior incidents. A recommendation engine and an unemployment-eligibility model are not the same governance problem, and treating them as one is the failure the assessment exists to prevent.
t_usecase.exam: Expect a stem describing an AI project and asking what is missing from the definition, or which readiness factor is absent. Three recurring distinctions: the business context is the environment while the use case is the specification; success metrics conflict, so naming one is a value choice rather than a technical default; and purpose limitation can bar data that is technically suitable. Use case assessment is a pre-development gate, so a question placing it after testing is testing whether you know the sequence.
key_points: Business context and use case are completed before requirements are frozen, and are documented deliverables
The use case specifies intended function, users and environments, assumptions and constraints, decision authority, lifetime and workload
Success metrics conflict with each other, so choosing one is a value judgment about which harm to accept
Data suitability fails on legal and ethical grounds as often as on technical ones; GDPR Article 5(1)(b) purpose limitation is the usual blocker
Decision rights are designed, not assumed: what the system decides alone, when a human is involved, how appeals work
Use case assessment is a pre-development gate, and rigour scales with decision impact and affected rights
Organizational readiness (leadership, data governance, security and privacy maturity, risk culture, expertise) is assessed before development starts

term:Use Case Assessment.deep_dive:
Use case assessment is the gate before development, and its job is to answer four questions: what domain is this, who could be harmed, is the data good enough, and does the problem need AI at all. The vault's Updating Policies for AI note sets out those criteria (societal context, potential harm, data quality, necessity of AI) and then requires a **classification level or risk rating** to be assigned at the onset of development, because the rating decides how much review follows.

The rating is not a formality. The note's low, medium and high tiers carry different actions: low gets standard review, medium gets enhanced documentation and review, and high gets third-party audits, external stakeholder input and executive sign-off. The EU AI Act formalises the same instinct with prescribed categories, which is why the note says to use low, medium or high where no formal classification exists. In ISO terms this is the **Clause 6.1.2 risk assessment** inside ISO/IEC 42001, and **ISO/IEC 42005** adds the mechanism that makes a rating operational: organization-defined thresholds that flag **sensitive uses** and **restricted uses** for escalation and formal approval.

The assessment is also where the frequency and rigour of later work is set. AI System Design lists the factors that drive it: decision impact, user exposure (internal or external), affected rights or opportunities, automation level (advisory or autonomous), the regulations that apply, and contextual factors such as prior incidents. A recommendation engine and an unemployment eligibility decision sit at opposite ends of that scale. Under the EU AI Act the assessment is what a provider relies on for the **Article 6(3)** derogation, and **Article 6(4)** requires it to be documented before the system goes on the market.
term:Use Case Assessment.exam_tip: Use case assessment is the pre-development gate: societal context, potential harm, data quality, necessity of AI, then a risk rating with proportionate controls. A high rating means third-party audit, external stakeholders and executive sign-off. ISO 42005 supplies the sensitive-use thresholds.

term:Use Case.deep_dive:
A use case is the point where an idea becomes governable, because it fixes the scope that every later control is measured against. ISO/IEC 22989 puts it at the front of the life cycle, in the **Adoption** phase alongside needs analysis, the feasibility study and requirements definition, and ISO/IEC 5338:2023 carries the same idea as AI system life cycle processes.

The scope elements are the examinable part, and the vault's AI System Design note lists them: **intended function** (classification, prediction, assistance, recommendation), **intended users and environments**, **assumptions and constraints**, **decision authority** (autonomous or human in the loop), and **expected lifetime, workload and frequency**. Under the EU AI Act these map onto **Article 3(12)**, the intended purpose, which is what the risk tier is assessed against, and **Article 3(13)**, reasonably foreseeable misuse. Annex III is effectively a list of use cases, so moving a system into an Annex III category is what makes it high risk under **Article 6(2)**.

Two consequences follow. First, scope creep is a compliance event, not just a project risk: a model built to forecast demand and later used to rate individual workers has changed its intended purpose, which is an **ISO/IEC 42005** reassessment trigger and can move the system into a high-risk category. The impact assessment record must therefore cover intended uses, unintended uses and reasonably foreseeable misuse, not only the planned purpose. Second, the data that supports the use case has to be lawful for it: **GDPR Article 5(1)(b)** purpose limitation means historical data cannot simply be reused for training without a lawful basis for the new purpose.
term:Use Case.exam_tip: A use case is a scope statement: function, users, constraints, decision authority, expected workload. Name the unintended uses too. Under the EU AI Act the intended purpose (Art. 3(12)) sets the risk tier, and a change of intended purpose is an ISO 42005 reassessment trigger.

term:Business Context.deep_dive:
Business context is the answer to "why this system, here, now", and ISO/IEC 42001 makes it an auditable requirement rather than a preamble. **Clause 4 (Context of the organization)** obliges the organization to determine the external and internal factors that affect the AIMS (4.1), identify interested parties and their needs and expectations (4.2), and define the scope and boundaries of the management system (4.3). **Clause 5.5** then requires the AI policy to sit on top of that context. The audit question is not whether a context document exists, but whether the planning in Clause 6 can be traced back to it.

Keep three neighbouring ideas apart, because the exam mixes them. **Business context** is the organizational, strategic and operational environment the system will live in. A **business case** is the statement of expected benefit to the organization. A **use case** is the high-level specification that translates the context into scope, data and outcomes. The vault's AI System Design note treats context as the input, the use case as the specification, and the impact assessment as the downstream check.

The context also fixes the legal tier. Under the EU AI Act the risk classification follows the **intended purpose**, so a context change can change the obligations: an Annex III system escapes high risk only through the **Article 6(3)** derogation, and **Article 6(4)** requires the provider to document that assessment before placing the system on the market. **Article 9** risk management must be run against the intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable misuse, which are context facts. Readiness belongs to the same question: leadership and budget, data governance maturity, cybersecurity and privacy maturity, risk tolerance, and access to legal, IT, data science and operations expertise.
term:Business Context.exam_tip: Context is auditable: ISO 42001 Clause 4 requires external and internal factors, interested parties and the AIMS scope. Keep business context (the environment), business case (expected benefit) and use case (the specification) apart. EU AI Act classification follows the intended purpose.

t_lifecycle.overview: Lifecycle documentation is the evidence trail from planning to decommissioning: requirements, design decisions and their rationale, training and testing records, traceability to audits, plus the management system that keeps it consistent (a QMS) and the system card that summarizes the result. Data integrity runs through all of it, because documentation is only evidence if the records have not been corrupted or silently altered.
t_lifecycle.deep_dive:
### Requirements come first

Before design, formally identify and capture requirements, and record their source, owner, priority and rationale. Each requirement must be verifiable, traceable, unambiguous and measurable. Categories include functional (what the system does), technical or non-functional (performance, scalability, security, privacy, usability, resilience), regulatory (what specific rules require), and security. Evaluation metrics are defined with thresholds (accuracy, calibration, latency, cost per inference), and the final set is approved by management. A useful discipline: stakeholders with organizational influence tend to dominate requirements-setting, so record who provided each requirement and deliberately include feedback from affected groups.

### Two dimensions of documentation

The **design and build process** is documented once and revised periodically; the **design of the system** is documented per system. A design baseline captures system purpose and scope, stakeholders and roles, ethical and regulatory considerations, boundaries and interfaces, data and model design, and risk and lifecycle management including fallback, monitoring, retraining and retirement plans. The development phase adds architecture diagrams with version control, code and model repositories with change history, tooling and dependency inventories, and security artifacts.

### Training and testing records

Training documentation covers data sources and characteristics (including exclusions and filtering, with the data archived and immutable), the labeling process and its quality assurance, training configuration and hyperparameters, performance benchmarks and the evidence behind chosen thresholds, bias detection and mitigation with its tradeoffs, and testing outcomes for robustness, generalization, privacy and security. Testing documentation covers methodology, whether test data was withheld from training, results with false positive and negative rates, stress and edge-case analysis, known failure modes and system behaviour on failure, and user testing. Under the EU AI Act the expectation is documentation sufficient to reproduce the design and development effort and to explain the design rationale years later.

### The QMS and the system card

A **quality management system** is the formalized set of processes, procedures and responsibilities that makes all of the above repeatable rather than improvised. ISO/IEC 42001 is the certifiable AI management system, and the EU AI Act requires a QMS from providers of high-risk systems (Article 17). The **system card** is the outward-facing artifact: broader than a model card, it describes the whole deployed system including architecture, training data, intended use, limitations and ethical considerations. Transparency obligations and instructions for use (Article 13) are what the card supports for downstream users.

### Traceability and integrity

Version control links code, data and documentation; requirements link to design elements, test plans and results; releases are tagged with the risk assessment that approved them; and decisions are recorded with their rationale and outcome, not just the decision. Data integrity is the prerequisite: if records, datasets or model artifacts can be altered without detection, the documentation proves nothing. That is why training data should be archived immutably, changes logged, and artifact repositories access-controlled and audited.
t_lifecycle.exam: Expect the artifact-to-purpose mapping: requirements specification (what was asked for), design baseline (why it was designed that way), training and testing records (what was done and what happened), system card (what the deployed system is), QMS (how all of it stays repeatable). The integrity angle is easy to miss: documentation is only evidence if it cannot be silently changed. Remember that ISO/IEC 42001 is the certifiable management system and EU AI Act Article 17 requires a QMS of high-risk providers, while the system card is broader than a model card.

term:System Card.deep_dive:
A system card documents the whole AI system, not only the model inside it. The distinction from a model card is scope: a model card covers a model's characteristics, intended uses, limitations, performance and ethical considerations, while a system card adds the surrounding machinery that changes real-world behaviour, including the components the model is wired to, guardrails and filters, tool and retrieval access, interfaces, deployment context, infrastructure and integration points. AI Risk Management and Assurance states the boundary directly: a system card is the broader documentation covering the entire AI system. The vault's AI System Design note lists model and system cards together as essential AI-specific development artifacts, and the Framework Recall Cards note puts it in one line: a model card documents a model, a system card does the same at whole-system level.

Two earlier artefacts supply the method. **Model Cards for Model Reporting** (Mitchell and others, 2019) proposed the structured model card, and **Datasheets for Datasets** (Gebru and others, 2018) proposed the equivalent for datasets, covering motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing, uses and distribution. A system card typically draws on both and adds the integration layer.

The regulatory versions are stricter. **EU AI Act Article 11** requires providers of high-risk systems to draw up and keep up to date the technical documentation in **Annex IV**, covering the system's general description, the development process and details of monitoring and functioning, and Article 11(1) as amended by the 2026 Omnibus lets small mid-caps use a simplified form. **Article 13** requires instructions for use that let a deployer interpret output, including capabilities and limitations, accuracy and robustness metrics, known risks, input specifications and human oversight measures. For general-purpose models, **Article 53(1)(d)** requires a public summary of training content, and **Article 50(2)** requires machine-readable marking of synthetic output.

A system card is a transparency instrument, and that is the governance point. It is how a deployer learns what the provider knows about limitations, and it is evidence in an audit, but it is not the same document as the Annex IV technical documentation and does not discharge that duty on its own.
term:System Card.exam_tip: A model card documents a model; a system card documents the whole system, adding components, guardrails, tools, interfaces and deployment context. The legally required version for high-risk systems is the Annex IV technical documentation under EU AI Act Art. 11, plus Art. 13 instructions for use.

term:Quality Management System (QMS).deep_dive:
Under the EU AI Act a QMS is not optional for a high-risk provider. **Article 16(1)** makes it a provider obligation, and **Article 17** specifies what it must contain: documented policies and procedures for the regulatory compliance strategy and conformity assessment, design and design control, design verification, development and quality control, examination, test and validation procedures, technical specifications and standards, data management systems, the **Article 9 risk management system**, the **Article 72 post-market monitoring system**, **Article 73 serious incident reporting**, communication with authorities and notified bodies, record-keeping, resource management and an accountability framework. The system must be proportionate to the organization's size and risk exposure, and as amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) the proportionate route in **Article 17(2)** extends to small mid-caps as well as SMEs.

The QMS also does compliance work. **Article 43** allows conformity assessment for most Annex III systems to be based on internal control, but the notified-body route (Annex VII) assesses the **QMS and the technical documentation**. So a thin QMS is not a paperwork gap, it is the thing the assessment is conducted against.

Keep the instruments apart, because the exam does. A **QMS** under Article 17 is a legal duty for high-risk providers. An **AI management system (AIMS)** under **ISO/IEC 42001:2023** is the certifiable, voluntary management-system standard built on the Annex SL clauses and the PDCA cycle; certification to it is a well-regarded way to evidence the Article 17 duty but is not the same thing. The **Article 9 risk management system** is one required component inside the QMS, not a substitute for it. **EN 18286:2026**, published July 2026, is the first CEN-CENELEC standard aimed at Article 17, but it gives a presumption of conformity only once its reference is published in the Official Journal under **Article 40(1)**.
term:Quality Management System (QMS).exam_tip: EU AI Act Art. 17 lists what a high-risk provider's QMS must contain, including the Art. 9 risk management system, Art. 72 post-market monitoring and Art. 73 incident reporting. ISO 42001 is the certifiable AI management system, not the QMS itself, and a QMS is what a notified body assesses under Art. 43.

term:Life Cycle.deep_dive:
The ISO definition is deliberately broader than software: the development of a system, product, service, project or other human-made entity **from planning through to decommissioning**. The clause "through to decommissioning" is the one to remember, because it is what makes documentation and monitoring obligations run to the end of service life rather than stopping at launch. ISO/IEC 22989 sets out the AI-specific model, and it is the backbone the other standards hang on: **Adoption** (needs analysis, feasibility, stakeholder engagement, requirements) to **Design and Construction** (data collection and preparation, model design, training, tuning) to **Verification and Validation** to **Deployment** to **Operation and Monitoring** to **Continuous Validation** to **Reassessment** to **Decommissioning**. ISO/IEC 5338:2023 carries the same phases as AI system life cycle processes, and ISO/IEC 23894 Annex C maps its risk processes onto them.

The EU AI Act uses the same span. **Article 9** makes the risk management system a continuous iterative process across the life cycle, not a pre-launch exercise. **Article 15** requires accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity at appropriate levels **throughout the life cycle**, and requires resilience to errors and faults and mitigation of feedback loops. **Article 72** requires providers of high-risk systems to run a post-market monitoring system. **Article 111(2)** ties the legacy transition to a significant change in the design of a system already on the market, so a mid-life redesign can bring an old system into the high-risk regime.

In practice the life cycle is why governance has stages rather than a single approval: requirements are baselined, design decisions recorded, training documented, testing evidenced, and monitoring maintained after go-live, with reassessment triggered by change rather than only by the calendar.
term:Life Cycle.exam_tip: ISO 22989 runs the AI life cycle from adoption to decommissioning, so duties do not end at launch. EU AI Act Art. 9 is iterative across the life cycle, Art. 15 applies throughout, and Art. 72 adds post-market monitoring. A significant mid-life change can trigger the high-risk regime.

term:Data Integrity.deep_dive:
Data integrity is the property that data has not been corrupted, altered or quietly replaced between collection and use. ISO/IEC 22989 lists **integrity** among the characteristics of trustworthiness, next to reliability, availability, security and authenticity, so it belongs to the same family that ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act draw on. Keep it apart from its neighbours: **data quality** is fitness for purpose (representative, complete, accurate for the task), **provenance** is the documented lineage of where the data came from, and **integrity** is the guarantee that what is being used is what was collected.

The legal hooks are specific. **EU AI Act Article 10** requires training, validation and testing datasets to be relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, **free of errors and complete**, with data governance covering collection, preparation, bias examination and gap identification. **GDPR Article 5(1)(d)** requires personal data to be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date, and **Article 5(1)(f)** requires integrity and confidentiality, meaning protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage. ISO/IEC 42001's data quality requirements (Annex B.7.4) expect data to be accurate, objective, precise, reliable, valid and labelled.

The practical failure mode is what makes integrity a governance issue rather than a storage issue: **data poisoning**, where an adversary alters training data to influence model behaviour, and **drift**, where the statistical properties of input data change so the model is fed something other than what it learned on. NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy (AI 100-2) catalogues poisoning alongside evasion and privacy attacks. Controls that answer to integrity include immutable or versioned datasets, access control and logging on data pipelines, validation and checksums on ingestion, and archiving training data unchanged so that a model can be reproduced and audited.
term:Data Integrity.exam_tip: Integrity (data unchanged) is not quality (data fit for purpose) or provenance (documented lineage). EU AI Act Art. 10 wants data free of errors and complete; GDPR Art. 5(1)(d) requires accuracy and 5(1)(f) integrity. Data poisoning and drift are the failures that make it a governance control.
